content: Elephant shrews, also known as jumping shrews, are small insectivorous mammals native to Africa. They belong to the family Macroscelididae within the order Macroscelidea. Their common English name originates from the resemblance of their elongated noses to an elephant's trunk and an assumed relationship with true shrews (family Soricidae) in the order Insectivora. However, it is now clear that elephant shrews are not closely related to true shrews. Some people prefer to call them sengis, a term derived from Bantu languages in Africa. These animals are widely distributed across southern Africa and can inhabit a variety of environments, ranging from the arid Namib Desert to rocky outcrops in South Africa and dense forests. One species, the North African Elephant Shrew, is found in the semi-arid, mountainous regions of the far northwest of the continent. Elephant shrews vary in size, measuring between 100 mm and 300 mm in length and weighing from just under 50 g to over 500 g. They are quadrupedal, with mouse-like tails and relatively long legs for their size. Their elongated noses, or trunks, vary in size among species but are all flexible and used to search for food. Their lifespan is typically two to three years. Their diet primarily consists of insects and other small invertebrates, such as beetles, spiders, worms, ants, and termites, which they forage from leaf litter. They also consume seeds and some green plant material. Elephant shrews possess large canine teeth and high-crowned cheek teeth, similar to those of ungulates. Their dental formula is distinctive. Although they are mostly diurnal and highly active, elephant shrews are elusive and rarely seen. They are cautious, well-camouflaged, and adept at escaping threats by dashing away. Some species create a network of cleared pathways through the undergrowth, which they patrol for insect prey. These pathways also serve as unobstructed escape routes when disturbed. Elephant shrews are not highly social animals, but many species form monogamous pairs that share and defend a home territory. They mark their territories using scent glands. Certain species, such as those in the genus Rhynchocyon, dig small conical holes in the soil to forage, while others use natural crevices or construct leaf nests. Females give birth to litters of one to three young several times a year, following a gestation period of 45 to 60 days. The young are relatively well-developed at birth but remain in the nest for several days before venturing outside. Historically, elephant shrews were classified alongside shrews and hedgehogs in the order Insectivora, considered distant relatives of ungulates, grouped with tree shrews, or even associated with hares and rabbits in the order Lagomorpha. However, recent molecular evidence strongly supports their inclusion in the superorder Afrotheria. This group unites elephant shrews with tenrecs, golden moles, and certain mammals previously thought to be ungulates, such as hyraxes, sirenians, aardvarks, and elephants. Several fossil species of elephant shrews have been discovered, all originating from Africa. Some, like Myohyrax, were so similar to hyraxes that they were initially misclassified as members of that group, while others, such as Mylomygal, were more rodent-like in appearance. These unusual forms became extinct by the Pleistocene epoch. Today, there are 16 recognized species of elephant shrews, distributed across four genera, two of which are monotypic.
